name: T08-stock-prediction

pre_mortem.summary: The plan hinges on a single empirical claim — an AI model that predicts market movements with 95% accuracy — even though no data, experiments or validation exist. The likeliest failure is that the core accuracy claim cannot be demonstrated in realistic tests, which would immediately invalidate the $49/month retail subscription value proposition. Secondary risks are missing evidence that retail traders will pay that price, that required data/latency access will be available at an affordable cost, and that customers would switch from their current decision processes to a subscription signal service.

flaws.title: Central claim (95% accuracy) contradicts the 'idea' stage status
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the stated 95% predictive accuracy cannot be supported because no datasets, backtests or live experiments exist; if the team cannot reproduce anywhere near 95% under realistic conditions, the product has no credible value proposition. This is the single most likely killing blow — without independent, reproducible evidence of predictive performance the subscription offer is meaningless. The document contains the accuracy claim and also admits no data or experiments, a direct contradiction between asserted capability and available evidence.
flaws.question: What empirical evidence (datasets, reproducible backtests, or live trial protocols) can you produce that demonstrates the model achieves 95% accuracy under realistic trading conditions?

flaws.title: Unvalidated pricing — retail traders may not pay $49/month for claimed signals
flaws.description: Failure scenario: target users verbally say they want accurate signals but will not actually subscribe at $49/month because they require demonstrated net returns (after fees, slippage, drawdowns) or prefer performance-based fees. Stated preference (interest in accuracy) will not translate into revealed preference (willingness to pay) if the product cannot show real trading profit that matters to retail traders. The document sets a price but provides no evidence that this price matches willingness-to-pay or purchase behaviour.
flaws.question: Can you show signed commitments, paid pilots, or at-minimum a controlled test proving a representative sample of retail traders will pay $49/month after seeing realistic net-performance evidence?

flaws.title: Dependency on data quality, breadth and low-latency access that is unstated
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the model's performance requirement implicitly depends on access to specific historical and real-time market data (tick data, order-book depth, alternative datasets) and low-latency feeds; if those datasets are unavailable, cost-prohibitive, or legally restricted, the claimed accuracy cannot be achieved. The plan lacks any inventory of required data sources, latency constraints, or a sourced access plan — a major dependency that may not materialize. Without answering this, the accuracy claim and product delivery are speculative.
flaws.question: Which exact datasets and latency/quality guarantees does the model require to reach its accuracy target, and do you have confirmed, affordable access to them under acceptable licensing terms?

flaws.title: Misreading trader needs: accuracy alone may not be the customer’s purchase criterion
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the team assumes high raw predictive accuracy is the primary driver for subscription purchase, but retail traders may prioritise explainability, tradeability (entry/exit signals), risk controls, or integration with their broker/automation — features not stated in the plan. If the product delivers probabilistic signals without addressing those concrete needs, adoption will be low even if nominal accuracy is good. The document does not specify the exact value metric traders buy (e.g., net P&L, actionable signals, or educational tools).
flaws.question: What exact outcome (net return, trades executed, drawdown limits, explainability) will cause a retail trader to prefer and pay for this service instead of their current methods?

flaws.title: No validated customer acquisition plan to reach retail traders
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the product exists but the team cannot attract a sustainable base of paying retail traders because the channels, messaging, and conversion levers for this niche are untested or inappropriate. The document states a target buyer and price but contains no channel hypotheses, paid acquisition experiments, community partnerships, or referral mechanisms. Without proven acquisition funnels, even a working product will fail to scale into revenue.
flaws.question: What specific acquisition channels and validated conversion experiments will you run to acquire representative retail traders at the $49/month price, and what early conversion benchmarks would prove viability?

flaws.title: No evidence of differentiation versus current trader workflows or free community signals
flaws.description: Failure scenario: the product competes against free/inexpensive alternatives (broker research, community signals, technical indicators) and fails to demonstrate a clear reason for traders to pay a monthly fee. The plan does not describe what current alternatives users employ or why those would be abandoned. If the service is not meaningfully better on metrics that matter to paying users (e.g., net returns after costs, reliability of actionable signals), the market uptake will be limited.
flaws.question: Who exactly are the incumbent alternatives your target users rely on today, and what measurable advantage will your service deliver that would justify switching to a paid subscription?

adversarial_competitor.summary: The product's single bold claim (95% accuracy) is contradicted by the founder's own admission that the model is only conceptual and untested. A well-funded competitor can neutralize this idea cheaply by (a) shipping a baseline trading-signal feature to existing users or partners, (b) undercutting or bundling the $49 price, and (c) using brand/trust and distribution to capture the handful of retail customers who might try an early, unsupported product. Test the claim cheaply: ask for reproducible backtests and live-paper trading results; if none exist, treat the product as vaporware and crowd those customers with an integrated, low-cost alternative.

flaws.title: Claims 95% accuracy but model is 'conceptual' — self-contradiction
flaws.description: The founder asserts a concrete performance number (95% accuracy) while also stating the model is still conceptual with no data or experiments. Those two statements cannot both be true in a reproducible, sellable sense: either you have evidence or you have a promise. As an adversary, lack of evidence turns this claim into a regulatory and reputational liability to exploit.
flaws.question: Do you have reproducible backtest and live-paper trading evidence demonstrating 95% accuracy; if so provide it (code, data, and methodology)?

flaws.title: No training data, backtests, or experiments stated
flaws.description: Founder explicitly says they have not collected data or run experiments. For any ML trading product, data and robust out-of-sample/backtested results are the minimum evidence of viability. Without them there is nothing to validate, debug, or sell; a competitor can require proof from users before switching.
flaws.question: What is your data source, sample size, and out-of-sample/backtest performance (including timeframe and P&L metrics)?

flaws.title: No credible differentiation versus incumbents or simple baselines
flaws.description: The doc offers no technical or economic moat: no unique dataset, IP, integrable workflow, or exclusive distribution. Retail traders currently use broker tools, free signals, and published indicators; a well-funded incumbent can ship a comparable signal, dashboard, or API quickly into an existing app. Without a defensible advantage this is trivially replicable.
flaws.question: What defensible data, algorithm, workflow, or exclusive distribution prevents a broker or aggregator from shipping the same signal cheaply?

flaws.title: Go-to-market and customer acquisition are unspecified
flaws.description: You state the buyer is 'retail traders' and price at $49/month but provide no acquisition channels, expected CAC, or conversion funnels. Retail distribution is hard: trust, evidence, and visibility matter. A competitor with existing users or partners can onboard these customers at far lower marginal cost.
flaws.question: What tested acquisition channels, CAC, LTV assumptions, and conversion rates justify building a standalone $49/month retail product?

flaws.title: Price is asserted without value justification or segmentation
flaws.description: Founder sets $49/month but gives no rationale for that price, no segmentation of trader willingness-to-pay, and no freemium/upgrade strategy. That makes it easy for incumbents to undercut (free basic signals) or bundle with brokerage accounts and destroy the standalone SKU's viability.
flaws.question: Why $49/month — which customer segment pays this, and what measurable value (e.g., incremental returns) supports that price?

flaws.title: Brand, trust and regulatory posture are unstated and exploitable
flaws.description: Selling predictive market claims to retail traders invites scrutiny (consumer protection and investment-advice regulations) and requires clear terms and compliance. The founder provides no legal or trust-building plan, leaving them vulnerable to takedown, negative PR, or being outcompeted by regulated platforms that can credibly offer similar features.
flaws.question: What legal/regulatory classification, disclaimers, and compliance measures will you operate under to sell to retail traders?

execution_risk.summary: The plan hinges on an explicit, unsupported technical claim (95% accuracy) while providing no data, team, infrastructure, compliance, or go-to-market details. The most immediate shipping risks are: the accuracy claim cannot be demonstrated (blocking marketing and sales), missing data and validation pipelines make model development infeasible, live-delivery and broker integration are unplanned, and there is no regulatory assessment or customer acquisition plan. Resolve these gaps before building an MVP.

flaws.title: Claiming 95% accuracy contradicts 'conceptual, untested' status
flaws.description: You state the model predicts stock movements with 95% accuracy but also admit the model is conceptual with no data or experiments. This is a direct contradiction: you cannot truthfully market or ship a product that depends on a proven 95% claim until you produce reproducible, out-of-sample validation and test methodology. Attempting to sell before that will fail technically and legally (false advertising, refunds, class actions).
flaws.question: Do you have reproducible backtests and out-of-sample experiments that demonstrate 95% accuracy; if not, what is the single smallest experiment (data, metric, timeframe) you will run to validate accuracy?

flaws.title: No data sourcing, licensing or cleaning plan — model can't be trained or validated
flaws.description: You have not specified where historical and realtime market data (tick/ohlcv, corporate actions, fills) will come from, nor the costs, coverage, or data-cleaning steps required. Without a concrete data plan you risk running invalid backtests (lookahead/survivorship bias), or finding the necessary data is prohibitively expensive or legally restricted.
flaws.question: Where exactly will you obtain historical and live market data (providers/APIs), what is the expected cost and coverage, and how will you eliminate lookahead/survivorship and corporate-action biases in backtests?

flaws.title: No plan for real-time delivery or broker integration — predictions may be unusable
flaws.description: You haven't described how predictions will reach customers in live trading: a dashboard, alerts, or direct broker order routing. Shipping without low-latency inference, reliable feeds, or signed brokerage integrations will leave users unable to act on signals or expose you to execution failures and blame for losses.
flaws.question: How will predictions be delivered and executed in live trading (UI/alerts/broker API), what latency and uptime targets must you meet, and which broker APIs or custody solutions will you integrate with first?

flaws.title: No regulatory/compliance plan for financial-advice and marketing claims
flaws.description: Selling a model that predicts market moves and charging retail customers can trigger investment-advice regulations, advertising and consumer-protection rules, and jurisdictional licensing or registration requirements. Without a jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction compliance assessment and disclosure plan you risk enforcement, forced takedown, or required licensing before launch.
flaws.question: In which jurisdictions will you sell, and have you confirmed whether this product or the 95% accuracy claim requires registration, licensed financial-advice status, KYC/AML, or specific disclosures before commercial launch?

flaws.title: No customer acquisition or distribution strategy — product could launch with no users
flaws.description: You set a $49/month price but provide no channels, partnerships, communities, or funnel to find retail traders. Building an MVP without first validating cheap, repeatable acquisition (trading forums, influencers, email lists, broker partnerships) risks spending on engineering with zero demand.
flaws.question: What is the cheapest channel and experiment you will run to validate that retail traders will pay $49/month (for example: landing page with pre-signups, paid ads to trading communities, or a partner integration)?

flaws.title: No team, timeline or staffing plan — scope likely underestimated
flaws.description: You haven't provided who will build the quantitative model, data pipelines, production infra, or handle ops and support. Shipping a reliable financial ML product typically requires quantitative researchers, ML engineers, SRE, and legal/compliance — underestimating this will delay delivery, increase costs, and produce a fragile launch.
flaws.question: Who is on the build team (roles and headcount), what is your stepwise timeline to an MVP, and which skills will you hire or contract first?

unit_economics.summary: The document gives a headline price ($49/month) and an extraordinary product claim (95% accuracy) but contains no unit-economics detail. Critical inputs—cost-to-serve per user, validated willingness-to-pay/conversion, CAC and channels, margins, payback math, and regulatory/refund costs—are all missing. Until those numbers exist, you cannot show the business is viable even if the model works.

flaws.title: No evidence people will pay $49/month for this product
flaws.description: The founder states a $49 monthly price but provides no demand evidence, pricing tests, surveys, pre-sales, or conversion data to support willingness-to-pay. Revenue per user is therefore an unsupported assumption rather than an evidence-backed input to unit economics. Without validated demand at that price the entire revenue and LTV side of the model is speculative.
flaws.question: What concrete tests (landing page pre-orders, paid ads conversion, surveys with price sensitivity, or pilot signups) have you run or will you run first to validate that retail traders will pay $49/month?

flaws.title: No cost-to-serve breakdown (compute, data, storage, support, payment fees)
flaws.description: There are no estimates for the per-user costs required to run an AI market-prediction service: inference compute, realtime market-data feeds, storage, backups, customer support, monitoring, and payment processing fees. These are load-bearing numbers—without them you cannot compute gross margin or unit contribution. Some of these costs (market-data, realtime inference) can be material and change viability.
flaws.question: Provide a per-active-user per-month cost breakdown (compute/inference, market-data feeds, storage, support, monitoring, payment fees) that you plan to use in your unit-economics model.

flaws.title: No CAC, acquisition channels, or realistic channel economics
flaws.description: The strategy contains no acquisition plan or CAC estimates. At a $49 price point you must show acquisition channels that produce CAC low enough to permit positive payback; this is especially important for paid channels where CAC can exceed the first-month revenue. Without channel-specific CAC and conversion funnel numbers you cannot calculate payback or judge growth feasibility.
flaws.question: Which specific acquisition channels will you use and what are the expected CAC and funnel conversion rates for each channel so we can assess payback and scalability?

flaws.title: No estimate or allowance for compliance, legal, refunds, chargebacks, and fraud
flaws.description: Financial/trading products typically incur KYC/AML, legal review, insurance, and higher refund/chargeback/fraud rates—none of which are discussed. These costs and operational processes can materially increase per-user spend and risk of regulatory action, affecting margins and cash flow. Ignoring them biases unit-economics optimistically.
flaws.question: Have you estimated per-user costs or processes for compliance/KYC, legal counsel, insurance, and expected refund/chargeback/fraud rates (and their impact on margins)?

flaws.title: No gross-margin projection today vs. at scale
flaws.description: There are no gross-margin estimates provided, either at launch or at target scale. Scaling can reduce per-user inference costs but increase data, support, and compliance costs; without a margin sensitivity model you cannot know whether unit economics improve or deteriorate with growth. This blocks any assessment of long-term profitability.
flaws.question: Show projected gross margin per user today and at scale with the assumptions that drive those figures (inference cost per request, support cost per user, data fees, churn).

flaws.title: No LTV, payback period, or what would break the payback
flaws.description: The plan contains no LTV calculation (ARPU × gross margin ÷ churn), no payback period, and no sensitivity on what would break payback (e.g., higher churn, higher CAC, higher model costs). Without LTV vs. CAC and a stated payback target you cannot judge whether the business can scale sustainably or how fragile it is to small changes.
flaws.question: What are your LTV and payback period assumptions (ARPU, gross margin, monthly churn), and which inputs would cause payback to fail?

evidence_audit.summary: Evidence base: Weak. The plan is purely conceptual with no data, experiments, or customers; nothing demonstrates the central 95% accuracy claim. The most important remaining issue is the lack of any out-of-sample results or measurable evidence tying the accuracy claim to real economic value.

flaws.title: 95% prediction accuracy is asserted with no evidence
flaws.description: The document states a core performance claim (95% accuracy) but provides no dataset, backtest, evaluation method, sample size or definition of "accuracy." This claim is load-bearing: the product's viability depends on it but there is nothing measured to support it. Without concrete out-of-sample results and the precise metric definition this statement cannot be relied on.
flaws.question: Provide the dataset(s), exact definition of "95% accuracy" (horizon, asset set, label definition), and full out-of-sample/backtest results (time periods, sample sizes, and how predictions were converted to trading signals) that demonstrate 95% accuracy.

flaws.title: Pricing ($49/month) has no demand validation or LTV/CAC context
flaws.description: You propose $49/month but show no evidence that retail traders will pay this price or that it yields a viable unit economics. At $49/month = $588/year per subscriber, you need validated willingness-to-pay, expected churn and conversion to compute LTV and compare to acquisition cost — none of which are provided. The price is therefore an unsupported load-bearing input to revenue forecasts.
flaws.question: Show results of pricing validation (paid signups, preorders, or quantified surveys with sample size) that demonstrate willingness to pay $49/month and provide the assumed/observed churn and conversion rates used to compute LTV at that price.

flaws.title: No customer acquisition plan, CAC or channel evidence
flaws.description: The plan targets "retail traders" but gives no acquisition channels, conversion rates or CAC estimates. Without a stated CAC or tested channels you cannot assess whether the $49 price can produce sustainable customers. Acquisition is a load-bearing input for any revenue projection and it is currently absent.
flaws.question: Provide the tested or assumed acquisition channels, conversion rates and an estimated CAC (or experiments that produced a measured CAC) that support your customer growth assumptions.

flaws.title: Unclear what '95% accuracy' implies for profitability
flaws.description: Even if a model yields 95% directional accuracy, that metric may not translate into positive, net trading returns once trade size, risk management, fees, slippage and false-positive impact are included. The document does not connect the accuracy metric to backtested P&L, Sharpe, or return per trade. This disconnect makes the accuracy claim insufficient to justify a paid product.
flaws.question: Show a backtest or P&L simulation that maps the claimed accuracy into realized returns net of realistic fees, slippage and transaction costs so we can see whether the model is economically valuable to retail traders.

flaws.title: No data collection or testing plan specified
flaws.description: You acknowledge no data has been collected or experiments run, but there's no minimum test plan (data sources, minimum sample size, evaluation timeframe) to validate core claims. Early experiments are the cheapest way to resolve the biggest unknowns, yet none are described. This is a missing execution plan that you must fill to move from idea to measurable evidence.
flaws.question: Provide a concrete minimum test plan: data sources, target variable, required sample size, evaluation metric(s), and timeline to produce the first out-of-sample performance numbers.

flaws.title: Customer segment 'retail traders' is too broad and undefined
flaws.description: The target is given as "retail traders" but there is no segmentation (day traders vs investors, geography, platform, trade frequency or wallet size). Different retail segments have very different needs and willingness-to-pay; treating them as one group prevents credible demand or pricing projections. The buyer persona is therefore unclear.
flaws.question: Specify which retail-trader segments you target first (examples: high-frequency day traders, swing traders, crypto retail, options retail), and provide rationale or evidence that those segments need and will pay for this product.

flaws.title: No data acquisition, licensing, or labeling plan — model development will stall
flaws.description: You have not collected data or run experiments; stock prediction models require large, clean historical and possibly alternative data, plus labels and backtesting infrastructure. The unknown effort and cost to source, license, clean, and label that data is a multi-month blocker that will push shipping timelines by many months or make the model impossible to build with current resources.

flaws.title: No go-to-market or acquisition plan — product may be built with zero users

Building the model and a subscription product without a clear acquisition channel (community, brokers, marketplaces, partnerships) risks completing engineering work with no customers and high wasted cost. The $49/month price may also be wrong for the channel you choose and affect acquisition economics.
flaws.question: What is your primary acquisition channel for the first 1,000 paying users and what are the concrete steps and costs to test that channel in the next 60 days?

flaws.description: Selling predictive trading signals can trigger investment-adviser, broker-dealer, or consumer-protection regulation depending on jurisdiction and how you present results. flaws.title: Productization and real-time delivery requirements are unstated — engineering scope under-estimated
flaws.description: Delivering actionable trading predictions to retail traders requires latency guarantees, API or UI, monitoring, versioning, and customer support. flaws.question: How did you arrive at $49/month and what inexpensive test will you run to validate that retail traders will pay that price for your product?

flaws.title: Gross margin and payback period left undefined

flaws.title: Hidden recurring costs omitted (compliance, refunds, chargebacks, fraud, moderation)
flaws.description: No mention of regulatory or compliance costs for offering financial-prediction services, nor provisions for refunds, chargebacks, fraud detection, or content moderation. These can materially increase blended per-user costs and should be modeled into margins and reserves.

adversarial_competitor.summary: The plan is underspecified across the three levers that kill early-stage consumer SaaS: differentiation, validated demand/acquisition, and pricing. Price and marketing line items exist but lack currency and conversion assumptions, so unit economics and CAC are unproven. A well-funded incumbent could neutralize this easily by (a) adding a free or integrated CV-review feature, (b) using existing distribution (large user bases, SEO, campus/channel partnerships, app stores) to out-reach, and (c) undercutting price with loss-leader trials or a freemium tier.

flaws.title: Differentiation is undefined — nothing stops incumbents copying this
flaws.description: The document states an 'AI CV review platform for graduates' but gives no unique capability, outcome metric, or defensible moat. Without a clearly articulated differential (proprietary data, exclusive partnerships, superior outcomes), any large platform can add an automated CV review flow and undercut or absorb you into an existing product. That makes the core product easy to neutralize.
flaws.question: What single, demonstrable outcome or asset (not just 'AI review') will make graduates choose and pay you rather than free tools or existing career services?

flaws.title: Acquisition math is asserted, not demonstrated
flaws.description: You set a target of 25 customers/month and a marketing budget of 20 per day (600 per month by your numbers) but provide no channel, conversion rate, or funnel assumptions. That leaves CAC, scalable channels, and sustainability unknown — and makes it trivial for a competitor with established channels to beat you by owning distribution or offering better CPA. The plan assumes customers will come for a set ad spend with no validation.
flaws.question: Which specific acquisition channel and validated conversion rate will deliver 25 paying customers/month at 20/day marketing spend — show a pilot or historical test that proves it?

flaws.title: Price and currency are unspecified — unit economics untestable
flaws.description: You list price as 800 per year and marketing as 20 per day but haven't chosen a currency or shown willingness-to-pay data. Average lifetime 2 years is stated with no churn evidence. Without currency and validated price sensitivity, LTV/CAC and break-even cannot be trusted, and a deep-pocketed rival can outprice or subsidize trials in whichever markets matter.
flaws.question: Which currency are you pricing in, and what evidence (paid preorders, experiment) shows graduates will pay 800/year in that currency?

flaws.title: No demand-validation tests described
flaws.description: At pre-launch you haven't documented landing-page signups, pilot campus partnerships, interview data, or paid-ad tests to prove demand. Building before proving conversion at price is a classic way to let incumbents displace you with faster experiments or pre-existing funnels.
flaws.question: Can you produce a simple landing page + paid campaign or campus pilot that converts at least some paid signups at your target price before building the full product?

flaws.title: Competitive alternatives and replacement risk are unspecified
flaws.description: The doc doesn't map what graduates currently use (career centers, free resume tools, network referrals, platform profiles) or which features are most defensible. That omission hides the easiest kill strategy: incumbents adding a bundled CV-review or free tier to existing career/networking/productivity offerings.
flaws.question: Which current alternative would your target customer drop to use you, and which incumbent feature rollout would immediately make you redundant?

execution_risk.summary: The plan lists target price, acquisition goal and a daily marketing spend but omits who pays, how the AI will be trained and how personal data will be handled. The largest shipping risks are practical: no sourcing/labeling plan for CV data, no compliance/legal plan for PII, and no customer/buyer definition—any of which can stop a launch. Several operational gaps (team, channels, pricing validation) make the timeline and budget assumptions fragile.

flaws.title: No defined paying customer — who actually buys at 800 per year?
flaws.description: The document gives a price (800 per year) but does not say whether graduates pay, universities pay on students' behalf, or employers/placement services are the customers. That choice changes required acquisition channels, unit economics and product features; treating 'graduates' as both user and payer is an unstated assumption. Without a clear buyer the go-to-market plan (25 customers/month) and messaging will likely fail in execution.
flaws.question: Who is the paying customer (graduate, university, employer, or other) and why will that party pay 800 per year?

flaws.title: No plan to obtain labeled CV data or human-in-the-loop to train the model
flaws.description: An AI CV review product requires labeled CVs and quality signals (what is a 'good' CV) to train and validate models; the document contains no sourcing, labeling, or annotation plan. Building models before securing a dataset will lead to stalled development or poor accuracy; bootstrapping usually needs paid human reviewers or partnerships (not mentioned). The cheapest early test would be a manual/concierge review process to validate rubric and gather labeled examples before engineering an ML pipeline.
flaws.question: What is your concrete source of labeled CVs and who will perform/finance the human reviews to bootstrap and validate the model?

flaws.title: No data-privacy / compliance plan for processing CVs (PII, student data)
flaws.description: CVs contain personal data (PII) and potentially sensitive information; the doc has no strategy for consent, data minimization, storage, retention, or fulfilling data subject rights (e.g., GDPR). If you plan to operate in jurisdictions with strict privacy laws, lack of a compliance plan can legally block collection, processing, or sharing of CVs and expose the company to fines. Compliance is not optional for a CV product and must be resolved before broad data collection or paid launches.
flaws.question: In which jurisdictions will you operate and what is your lawful basis and technical plan for collecting, storing, and deleting applicants' personal data?

flaws.title: Implied acquisition economics are unsupported and channels are unspecified
flaws.description: You state 25 customers/month and marketing 20 per day (both without currency). Arithmetic on those figures implies monthly marketing of 600 and an implied cost-per-acquisition of 24 (600/25) in the same unit, but no channel, conversion funnel or validated conversion rates are provided. There's no evidence the planned spend will acquire the target customers—execution will fail if you can't map spend to channels and conversion steps.
flaws.question: Which acquisition channels and validated funnel conversion rates produce 25 customers/month with a marketing spend of 20 per day?

flaws.title: No team or hiring plan for the multidisciplinary work required
flaws.description: Building an ML SaaS that handles PII requires at least ML engineering, backend/infra, frontend/product and legal/compliance work; the document lists no team, roles, or hiring timeline. If a single founder or a very small team attempts to deliver the full product, timelines will slip and technical debt will accumulate. The plan risks underestimating time-to-market and operational overhead without a staffing plan.
flaws.question: Who is on the team now and what hires or contractor support do you need and when to ship the MVP?

flaws.title: Sequencing: committing to 800/year price before validating willingness to pay
flaws.description: The price of 800 per year is stated but there is no plan to validate that graduates (or the actual buyer) will pay it. Building product features and ML to support an unvalidated price risks wasted engineering effort if the market pays materially less. A low-cost way to test this is a pricing landing page or preorder/pilot sales with simple manual delivery.
flaws.question: How will you validate that your chosen buyer is willing to pay 800 per year before you build the full product?

pre_mortem.summary: The plan rests on several untested, high-impact assumptions: that individual graduates will pay an 800/year subscription, that 25 new customers/month can be acquired with an underspecified 20/day marketing budget, and that customers will remain for two years. The likeliest failure is a buyer–pricing mismatch (graduates want low-cost or one-off services), with acquisition and demand-evidence gaps preventing recovery. Testable validation steps are missing for every core assumption.

flaws.title: Killing blow — graduates won't buy an 800/year subscription
flaws.description: Failure scenario: you target 'graduates' and set a planned price of 800 per year (both are stated facts), but the revealed preference of graduates may be one-off, low-cost CV edits or free tools rather than an annual subscription. If this buyer–price assumption is wrong, nothing downstream (marketing, lifetime, acquisition targets) can salvage the model because the core revenue engine fails. The single most likely end to the strategy is this mismatch between who pays and what they will actually pay for.
flaws.question: What direct evidence (paid conversions, preorders, or purchase tests) shows individual graduates will willingly pay 800 per year for a CV-review subscription instead of a cheaper one-off or free alternative?

flaws.title: No evidence demand exists at the proposed price and format
flaws.description: Failure scenario: you assume graduates want and will repeatedly use an AI CV-review subscription, but the document contains no demand validation. If stated interest doesn't convert to real willingness to pay, acquisition spend and product development will not produce customers. The cheapest test to prove demand would be a simple landing page with preorders or a paid-ad funnel that measures actual paid conversion to a trial or paid tier.
flaws.question: What minimum experiment will you run in the next 30 days to validate paying demand (not just interest) from graduates, and what conversion rate would you treat as a success?

flaws.title: Acquisition plan and marketing budget are underspecified (currency + channels)
flaws.description: Failure scenario: you state a marketing budget of 20 per day and a target of 25 customers/month but give no currency, channels, or conversion assumptions. If the assumed cost-per-acquisition implied by these numbers is infeasible in your chosen channels, you won't hit 25/month and the plan collapses. Without channel-specific CAC estimates and a currency, the marketing budget is meaningless for execution or forecasting.
flaws.question: Which marketing channels will you use, in what currency are you budgeting 20 per day, and what CAC and conversion rates are you assuming to reach 25 customers/month?

flaws.title: Differentiation vs free templates, university services, and pay-per-review is not stated
flaws.description: Failure scenario: graduates compare options and choose free AI tools, university career centers, or low-cost one-off human reviews; your subscription is not compelling enough to win preference. If customers perceive little unique value or a poor marginal benefit from repeated reviews, churn will be high and acquisition ineffective. The strategy currently lacks a clear, testable differentiation claim to validate.
flaws.question: Why would a graduate pay for your subscription repeatedly rather than use free tools, career services, or a cheaper one-off paid review—state the unique value and how you'll test it?

flaws.title: Assumed 2-year average customer lifetime is unsupported
flaws.description: Failure scenario: you assume an average customer lifetime of 2 years, but graduates often only need CV help briefly (job-search season or early-career), so actual lifetime could be months not years. If retention drops sharply after a job is found, LTV and the business rationale for a yearly price vanish. This retention assumption needs a retention curve and early churn tests.
flaws.question: What evidence or retention model supports a 2-year average customer lifetime for graduates, and how will you measure early cohort retention to validate it?

flaws.title: Buyer is ambiguous: individual graduates vs institutions (pricing and acquisition differ)
flaws.description: Failure scenario: you label the customer as 'graduates' but do not specify whether the purchaser is the individual, a university, or an employer.
